The most useful object in our apartment building was a brown chair that nobody wanted. It stood on the half landing between the second and third floors, directly beneath a window painted shut since at least the invention of margarine. The chair had a split in its vinyl seat. In summer the edges of the split pinched bare thighs, a fact every child in the building learned once and remembered forever. On the underside, in blue ballpoint, someone had written DENNIS. Nobody knew whether Dennis had owned the chair or merely been the last person willing to crawl under it.

On Tuesday evenings Mrs. Vale sat there halfway up with her groceries. She could manage the stairs or she could manage a conversation, but not both, so if you met her climbing you had to wait for the chair before telling her anything interesting. This gave the news a pleasing ceremonial quality. You carried it beside her, along with the bag containing the tins, while she gripped the rail and concentrated. Then she would sit, arrange her skirt over her knees, and say, “Well?” Even the announcement that the corner shop had run out of eggs felt worth the climb.

One February morning the chair disappeared. In its place was a rectangle of cleaner linoleum and a single blue thread. Somebody taped a note to the window: WHERE IS CHAIR? The missing article made the question sound urgent and international, as though embassies had already been notified. By lunchtime a second hand had added WHICH CHAIR? This was generally considered a poor joke, although my father maintained for years that it was a legitimate request for information. There were, he pointed out, millions of chairs. My mother asked how many of them he thought ordinarily lived outside our front door.

For three days people offered substitutes. A scarlet footstool appeared first, too low for Mrs. Vale to rise from without assistance. Next came a folding garden chair that closed around its occupant with the brisk discretion of a dentist drawing a curtain. Someone contributed a piano bench; someone else took it back to practice scales. Meanwhile the notes multiplied. One tenant blamed the landlord, another blamed teenagers, and a third proposed buying a replacement together. Under this proposal Mr. Levin wrote that he would happily contribute provided the new chair was not brown. We discovered strong feelings about municipal orange.

I was eleven and eager to investigate. My friend Ada had a magnifying glass, which we carried conspicuously despite finding nothing small enough to require it. We knocked on every door and asked when the resident had last seen the chair. Answers varied from yesterday to eighteen months ago. A man on the fourth floor said he had never seen it, then described it accurately enough to make himself our principal suspect. Ada suggested a trap. I suggested biscuits. We went downstairs to her kitchen and ate six ginger biscuits while discussing whether the police were allowed to have favorites.

On Saturday we found the chair in the laundry room. It was upside down on a blanket beside the boiler, with its four feet pointing toward a row of drying socks. Mr. Okafor from the ground floor was kneeling over it, easing tiny brass tacks out of the seat with a screwdriver. He had seen the split grow wider, he explained, and had taken the chair downstairs to mend it. Why hadn't he left a note? He looked honestly surprised. He had expected to finish before breakfast. Then the wood beneath the vinyl had turned out to be rotten too.

He showed us the old seat board. It came apart between his fingers like wet cardboard. The new one was cut from a cupboard door his sister had left in his cellar after remodeling her kitchen. One side was painted a brilliant yellow. This would face downward, he said, so nobody would know. Ada and I exchanged a glance. Here was precisely the kind of information that justified an investigation. We helped stretch green fabric across the seat, pulling opposite corners until our knuckles paled, while he drove in the tacks. The fabric had once been his good winter coat.

We carried the chair upstairs that afternoon. Mrs. Vale tried it first, although it was not Tuesday and she had no groceries. She settled herself, shifted experimentally, and pronounced the seat half an inch too high. Mr. Okafor said he could shorten the legs. She said he would do no such thing; she was making an observation, not lodging a complaint. Several people came out to admire the work. Mr. Levin liked the green. My father examined the window notes and admitted that, under the circumstances, WHICH CHAIR? had probably been an unnecessary question. Nobody claimed responsibility for writing it.

Years later, visiting my parents, I found a boy lying on his back beneath the chair. His shoes stuck out across the landing. For one absurd second I thought he was repairing a complicated piece of machinery, perhaps draining its oil. Then he wriggled free and asked me if I knew about the yellow. I told him I did. He looked disappointed, so I asked if he knew about Dennis. Within seconds he was back underneath, inspecting the rails. I waited with my shopping bag against my ankle until he emerged, dusty and triumphant, having found all six faded letters.

I almost told him everything: the cupboard door, the coat, the notes, the ginger biscuits. Instead I sat down. I had forgotten how much easier it was to talk to somebody on that landing when neither person was trying to get somewhere else. The boy had a theory that Dennis was a carpenter who signed all his work in secret. Why in secret? Because otherwise, he explained patiently, people would keep asking him to make things. Upstairs my mother opened her door and called to see what was keeping me. “News,” I called back, and stayed to hear the rest.
